transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Well, I... I guess I'm here because my mom made the appointment, honestly. But she's right, I suppose. It's just... I don't know how to explain it. It's like someone pulled the plug on everything, you know? I just don't care about anything anymore. And I mean *anything*. I used to take these community college art classes—watercolor, mostly, because I liked how unpredictable it was—but now my paints are just sitting there drying out on the desk and I can't even bring myself to look at them. And it's not just the art. I had this whole group of friends I'd play board games with every Thursday night. We'd order pizza and play Settlers of Catan or whatever, and I haven't gone in months. They keep texting, but I just leave them on read. Even getting outside... I used to love hiking up at the state park, or I was thinking about getting back onto this recreational soccer team I used to play for, but now? The thought of putting on my cleats or lacing up my hiking boots just feels impossible. It's like I'm made of lead. So I just sit in my room. All day, mostly. Just sitting there, watching the dust motes in the air, while my whole life just sort of... slips away. I know it's happening, but I can't find a single ounce of energy or care to stop it. It's just gone.
How long have you been feeling this way?

Well, it's... I mean, time is sort of a blur these days, but I know exactly when it really took hold. It was right after the divorce. Which has been... let's see, it's been about a year and eleven months now. Almost two years of this. I remember because the final papers came through in the mail, and everyone kept telling me it was a 'fresh start' or a 'new chapter' or whatever clichés people use when they don't know what else to say to you. 

But instead of a fresh start, it was like the book just ended. I had moved all my boxes back into my mom's house—which is why she's so involved and making my appointments now—and I remember just sitting on the edge of the bed in my old childhood room, looking at this stack of cardboard boxes. We had to divide up all our stuff, which was an absolute nightmare, especially the kitchen stuff and the books because we both bought so many books when we were together, and trying to remember who actually paid for what just felt so petty... but anyway, I was sitting there on the bed, and that heavy, lead feeling I was telling you about just sort of dropped right onto my shoulders. 

At first, I figured, well, I'm just grieving the marriage, right? It's normal to be sad when your life falls apart. You're supposed to stay in bed and cry for a few weeks. But the sadness never lifted. It just morphed into this giant, empty weight that drained everything else away. So, yeah... a year and eleven months. A year and eleven months of just sitting there while the days bleed into each other and my mom worries herself sick about me.
Have there been any periods over the last two years when you felt somewhat better, even if just for a little while?

Well... better is sort of a tricky word, isn't it? I mean, what is better? But... yeah, I guess there was a stretch. Before the absolute worst of this heaviness set in, before I stopped leaving my room entirely. It was right after I moved back in with my mom, when I was still trying to pretend I could handle things. I was still cooking sometimes—I remember I made this huge batch of minestrone soup because my mom loves it, and I actually went to the store and picked out the zucchini and the carrots and everything. I was even answering my friends' texts then. Not all of them, but some. I'd say, 'Yeah, I'm hanging in there,' or 'Thanks for checking in.' 

But the thing is, even then, even when I was standing at the stove stirring the soup or typing on my phone... I wasn't really okay. Because that was when the voice started. I was already hearing it. Just this... this murmur at first, and then it got clearer, telling me things I didn't want to hear. And the lights in the hallway of my mom's house—the way they flickered when the AC kicked on—I knew they weren't just flickering. I knew they were signals. About me. Like someone was trying to tell me something, or warn me, or maybe they were watching me. I spent weeks just staring at those hallway lights, trying to decode them while the voice just kept talking. So, I was functioning better, I guess, on the outside. I was making soup and texting. But inside... inside I was already gone into all of that, for weeks, before the depression just came down and crushed whatever was left of me.
Can you describe if and when you first noticed losing interest or pleasure in activities that you used to enjoy, like your art or spending time with friends?

Well, like I was saying about that time I was still trying to function... the real shift, when the bottom just completely fell out of everything I used to enjoy, that happened around the following summer. The summer after the divorce, I mean. 

I remember it so clearly because the heat was just oppressive that year, and my mom had the air conditioning running non-stop. I had actually brought my watercolors out to the dining room table one afternoon. I was thinking, you know, maybe I'll paint her garden. She has these massive hydrangeas out back, these huge blue and purple blooms, and I used to just love trying to mix the exact right shade of blue to match them. I had my little water cup ready, I had my brushes all laid out perfectly on a paper towel so I wouldn't stain her antique table—she's incredibly protective of that table because it was my grandmother's—and I just... I just sat there. 

I stared at the blank paper, and the brush suddenly felt like it weighed a hundred pounds. I realized in that exact moment that I didn't care about the hydrangeas. I didn't care about the colors, or the water, or any of it. And the thought of my friends texting me to play board games later that week... it just made me feel so profoundly exhausted that I wanted to weep, but I couldn't even muster the energy to cry. 

That was when the depression just became completely constant. It just locked in, like a vault door shutting. So that would make it... gosh, about a year and four months ago? Yes, a year and four months. It's been exactly like that, just this constant, unrelenting nothingness for a year and four months now. I actually just left all those paints sitting right there on the dining table until my mom finally packed them away in a plastic bin weeks later because she needed the space for her sewing machine, and I didn't even care that she put them away. I haven't touched them, or really wanted to do anything at all, since that day.
Have you been feeling this way—like you don’t care about anything and can’t bring yourself to do the things you used to enjoy—nearly every day, for most of the day, for the past two years?

Well, yes. Yes, I have. I mean, it's not just a passing thing, you know? It's not like I wake up and think, 'Oh, I'm having a bad day today,' and then tomorrow I'm fine and I want to go to a movie or something. It's... it's every day. Most of the time since this illness, or whatever this is, really took over... I haven't just been scared by the voice, or confused by the lights in the hallway, though that's awful, of course. It's the other part. I've just been so deeply, fundamentally depressed. 

It's like... it's like I'm barely interested in anything at all. The entire world just feels completely gray and pointless. And it's not just that I don't want to paint or see my friends, it's that the very idea of doing those things feels impossible. Like I'm standing at the bottom of a well and everyone else is up at the top, and they're throwing down ropes, but I don't even have the energy to lift my arms to grab them. 

And my mom, she tries, she really does. She'll come into my room and open the blinds—which I hate, because the light just feels too loud, if that makes sense—and she'll say, 'Let's go for a walk, just to the end of the block and back.' And I just look at her, and I think... what's the point? What is the point of walking to the end of the block? The block is just concrete and grass, and then you just have to walk back, and you're still exactly where you started, just more tired. 

So, yes. Nearly every day, for most of the day, for the past year and four months, ever since that day with the hydrangeas. And even before that, it was building up to it. It just feels... it feels like my life is already over, and I'm just sitting here in my childhood bedroom waiting for the rest of my body to catch up with the fact that I'm already gone. It's exhausting, honestly. Just existing is exhausting.
Have you ever experienced a period of time when your mood was elevated, you felt unusually energetic, or you didn’t need much sleep, even if others around you noticed it was out of character for you?

Elevated? Energetic? No... no, I don't think I even know what that feels like. Honestly, it sounds like you're describing a completely different person, or maybe a character in a movie or something, because that is so far from anything I've ever experienced. 

You mentioned not needing much sleep... I mean, sleep is basically the only thing I actually want to do. If I could just sleep for twenty-four hours a day, I think I would. My mom actually came into my room just yesterday—or maybe it was Tuesday? I completely lose track of the days now because they all just blend together into this one long, gray stretch—but she came in and asked if I was ever going to get out of bed because it was almost three in the afternoon. And I wasn't even fully asleep at that point, I was just lying there under this heavy duvet she bought me for Christmas a couple of years ago, the one with the little pale blue flowers on it. I was just lying there staring at the dust on the blades of the ceiling fan, wishing I could just drift off again so I wouldn't have to be awake and conscious of how heavy my limbs felt. 

So the idea of having extra energy, or feeling unusually good or elevated... no. I can't even imagine waking up and feeling like I have the energy to just exist, let alone do extra things. The most energetic I've felt in years was when I made that minestrone soup I told you about, and even then, it wasn't like I was buzzing or hyper or anything like that. It was just a normal amount of effort that ended up completely draining me for days afterward. 

I've never had a time where I felt unusually happy or like I didn't need to rest. It's always just been this dragging weight. Like I'm trying to walk through wet cement, all the time. Even back when I was taking a few college classes, before everything really fell apart and I had to stop working and move back home, I was never the type to stay up all night with endless energy. I've always desperately needed my sleep, and lately, it's like my body is just made of lead. So, no, absolutely nothing like what you're describing. I almost wish I did have a little bit of that energy, to be honest with you. Maybe then my mom wouldn't look so heartbroken and worried all the time when she comes in to collect my laundry from the floor. But no, it's just the exhaustion. Always just the exhaustion.
Have you noticed any significant changes in your appetite or weight over the past year?

I mean, yes, actually. A lot. It’s funny you ask that because my mom was just commenting on it the other day when she was doing the laundry. She held up my favorite pair of jeans—these dark wash Levi's I bought a couple of years ago when I was still trying to keep up appearances and go out sometimes—and she said they looked like they belonged to a teenager. And she's right, because I put them on last week to go to the pharmacy, and they were so loose I actually had to take a hair tie and knot the waistband just to keep them from sliding right off my hips while I was walking down the aisle to get my mom's vitamins. 

It's just... I don't know, eating feels like such a chore now. I'll go almost the entire day without having a single bite of anything. My mom will make these beautiful meals, like she made a roast chicken with rosemary and lemon on Sunday, and the smell filled the whole house, but when she put a plate in front of me, I just stared at it. I took one bite of the chicken, and it honestly tasted like cardboard. It was just this dry, tasteless mass in my mouth that I had to force myself to chew and swallow. 

I used to love food, you know? I used to love cooking and baking. I told you about that minestrone soup, but before that, I used to bake these intricate layer cakes for my friends' birthdays. I’d spend hours making Swiss meringue buttercream and piping little roses. I’d taste everything as I went, making sure the vanilla extract was just right. But now... now I look at food and I just feel completely indifferent. Sometimes the thought of eating actually makes me feel a little nauseous, just because of the sheer effort it takes to chew and digest. 

So, most days, I just don't eat until maybe six or seven at night, and even then, it's usually just a piece of dry toast or maybe half an apple if my mom practically begs me to eat some fruit. I've definitely lost a lot of weight. I don't have a scale in my room—my mom took it out because she said I was obsessing over the numbers before, when I was feeling really paranoid about things—but I can feel it in my bones. My collarbones stick out now, and when I lie in bed, I can feel my hip bones pressing into the mattress. It's just another part of me fading away, I guess. Just like everything else.

I took one bite of the chicken, and it honestly tasted like cardboard. It was just this dry, tasteless mass in my mouth that I had to force myself to chew and swallow. 

I used to love food, you know? I used to love cooking and baking. I told you about that minestrone soup, but before that, I used to bake these intricate layer cakes for my friends' birthdays. I’d spend hours making Swiss meringue buttercream and piping little roses. I’d taste everything as I went, making sure the vanilla extract was just right. But now... now I look at food and I just feel completely indifferent. Sometimes the thought of eating actually makes me feel a little nauseous, just because of the sheer effort it takes to chew and digest. 

So, most days, I just don't eat until maybe six or seven at night, and even then, it's usually just a piece of dry toast or maybe half an apple if my mom practically begs me to eat some fruit. I've definitely lost a lot of weight. I don't have a scale in my room—my mom took it out because she said I was obsessing over the numbers before, when I was feeling really paranoid about things—but I can feel it in my bones. My collarbones stick out now, and when I lie in bed, I can feel my hip bones pressing into the mattress. It's just another part of me fading away, I guess. Just like everything else.
